newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to tighten rule on mine cleanup costs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to tighten rule on mine cleanup costs.

text.p: Beginning Friday, all U.S. mines on public lands will be responsible for 100 percent of the costs of restoring the public land that they have disturbed, no matter how small an area of the government-held lands their operations are on.
The Interior Department will publish a final rule in the Federal Register on Friday on so-called hard rock bonding. Hard rock mining operations mine gold, silver, copper and diamonds.

The new rule will require all miners to maintain financial guarantees or bonds for 100 percent of the cleanup costs of the public lands they are working on, and will take effect immediately, an Interior Department official said.
Previously, miners whose operations are on less than 5 acres of public land have been exempt from having to post a bond for the entire costs of any necessary cleanup.

Supporters of ongoing mining reform efforts applauded the new law, noting that about 80 percent of the almost 7,000 hard rock mines on public lands operate on five acres or less, and that it costs the government many billions of dollars to restore land that has been mined.

"There are now about 500,000 sites on public land that have been abandoned at one time or another by miners who did not restore the land and 2,000 in national parks ... the government is left with contaminated sites to clean up," said a Democrat staff member of the House Resources Committee.
